episodes.title: How we built Grok Bot in a month | Roman Ugarte (SpaceXAI)
episodes.description:
Roman Ugarte helped incubate and build Grok Bot, the popular new knowledge-work agent from SpaceXAI. A small, isolated team took it from first line of code to a working internal product in four weeks, and to a hugely successful public launch just three weeks later. Before Grok Bot, Roman led Growth at Cursor, where he helped scale the company from 15 people to over 1,000 before its acquisition by SpaceX.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. The origin story of Grok Bot
2. The key decision to build it from scratch instead of adding it to Cursor
3. Why the team personally onboarded nearly 300 of its first users
4. The two early product decisions that made Grok Bot so successful
5. Their “colleague-pilled” product philosophy
6. Roman’s advice on moats, and what has allowed Cursor to keep winning in the most competitive market in the world
episodes.descriptionCN:
Roman Ugarte 帮助孵化和构建了 Grok Bot，这是 SpaceXAI 推出的流行的新型知识工作代理。一个小型的、孤立的团队在四个星期内将其从第一行代码变成了一个可运行的内部产品，并在三周后取得了巨大成功的公开发布。在加入 Grok Bot 之前，Roman 领导了 Cursor 的发展，在该公司被 SpaceX 收购之前，他帮助该公司从 15 人扩大到 1,000 多人。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. Grok Bot 的起源故事
2.关键决定是从头开始构建它而不是添加到Cursor中
3. 为什么团队亲自吸引了近 300 名第一批用户
4. 让 Grok Bot 如此成功的两个早期产品决策
5. 他们的“同事堆积”的产品理念
6. Roman 关于护城河的建议，以及是什么让 Cursor 在全球竞争最激烈的市场中不断获胜

episodes.title: Why companies are becoming a series of loops | Anish Acharya (a16z)
episodes.description:
Anish Acharya is a General Partner at Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), where he has focused on consumer investing. Anish is one of the most insightful, thought-provoking, and in-the-weeds product investors I’ve met, and this conversation will get your mind buzzing. Before joining a16z, Anish was a serial founder and operator: he founded SocialDeck, which he sold to Google, then led multiple efforts inside Google before founding Snowball, which he sold to Credit Karma. At Credit Karma he rose to VP of Product and then GM of the consumer product and the broader credit card business.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why you don’t have to worry about becoming part of the “permanent underclass”
2. Why company building will now involve creating a series of loops
3. What’s happening in consumer right now
4. Why the biggest opportunity in consumer is “/loop, make me happier”
5. Why moats are discovered, not designed
6. The rising importance of distribution as a moat
7. Being a model sommelier
episodes.descriptionCN:
Anish Acharya 是 Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) 的普通合伙人，专注于消费者投资。安尼什是我见过的最有洞察力、最发人深省、最活跃的产品投资者之一，这次谈话会让你头脑发热。在加入 a16z 之前，Anish 是一位连续创始人和运营商：他创立了 SocialDeck，并将其卖给了 Google，然后在 Google 内部领导了多项工作，最后创立了 Snowball，并将其卖给了 Credit Karma。在 Credit Karma，他升任产品副总裁，然后担任消费产品和更广泛的信用卡业务总经理。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么你不必担心成为“永久下层阶级”的一部分
2. 为什么公司建设现在需要创建一系列循环
3. 消费者现在正在发生什么
4. 为什么消费者最大的机会是“/loop，让我更快乐”
5. 为什么护城河是被发现的，而不是设计的
6. 分销作为护城河的重要性日益增加
7. 成为模范侍酒师

episodes.title: AI’s third era: the rise of persistent AI coworkers | Tara Seshan (Product Lead ChatGPT Work)
episodes.description:
Tara Seshan leads product for Codex and ChatGPT Work at OpenAI (alongside previous podcast guest Andrew Ambrosino, who’s her engineering manager). Before OpenAI, Tara spent over six years at Stripe, where she joined as one of the first five product managers. She went on to lead product for Watershed, which Time magazine named one of the best inventions of 2022, and she is also a founder and Thiel Fellow. Most personally meaningful to me: Tara is one of the three inaugural Lenny’s Newsletter Fellows, a program I ran a couple of years ago to spotlight the most exciting up-and-coming product leaders.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. The shift from “rowing” to “steering,” and why human judgment and ambition will become differentiators as AI takes on execution
2. How OpenAI thinks about building for model capabilities two to three months out
3. OpenAI’s best internal memes, such as “Is this maximally accelerated?” and “Are you mainlining it yet?”
4. Why ambition is the new bottleneck for companies, and why elevating others’ ambitions is now the key part of the PM job
5. Writing as thinking vs. writing as reporting
episodes.descriptionCN:
Tara Seshan 在 OpenAI 领导 Codex 和 ChatGPT Work 的产品（与之前的播客嘉宾 Andrew Ambrosino 一起，他是她的工程经理）。在 OpenAI 之前，Tara 在 Stripe 工作了六年多，她是该公司首批五名产品经理之一。她继续领导 Watershed 的产品，该产品被《时代》杂志评为 2022 年最佳发明之一，她也是创始人和 Thiel Fellow。对我个人来说最有意义的是：Tara 是首届 Lenny’s Newsletter Fellow 的三名成员之一，这是我几年前运行的一个项目，旨在关注最令人兴奋的新兴产品领导者。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 从“划船”到“掌舵”的转变，以及为什么随着人工智能的执行，人类的判断力和野心将成为差异化因素
2. OpenAI 如何考虑两到三个月后的模型能力构建
3. OpenAI 最好的内部模因，例如“这是最大加速吗？”和“你已经把它主线化了吗？”
4. 为什么野心是公司的新瓶颈，为什么提升他人的野心现在是 PM 工作的关键部分
5. 作为思考写作与作为报告写作

episodes.title: How to close $100K+ enterprise deals, step by step | Jen Abel
episodes.description:
Jen Abel is the co-founder of JJellyfish and GM of enterprise sales at State Affairs. She is widely regarded as one of the sharpest practitioners in enterprise sales, and for that reason, this is her third visit to the podcast. In our first conversation we went deep on founder-led sales; in our second we mapped the $1M–$10M playbook. This time we do something I’ve never seen on another podcast: walk step by step through the full enterprise sales cycle. Most people think it’s five steps. Jen shows it’s closer to 15.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why the standard five-stage CRM pipeline is a forecasting tool, not a sales process, and what the real 15-step cycle looks like
2. The “pincer model” for landing the first meeting at the executive and N-minus-one level simultaneously
3. How to craft a two-to-three-sentence message around giving them “alpha”
4. How to run an intro call that extracts maximum intelligence before you ever show a demo
5. The two-to-three-day pilot structure, how to define success jointly, and when to charge for a longer pilot versus giving it away
6. Navigating pricing, procurement, redline negotiations, and the final signature without losing momentum
episodes.descriptionCN:
Jen Abel 是 JJellyfish 的联合创始人兼国务部企业销售总经理。她被广泛认为是企业销售领域最敏锐的从业者之一，因此，这是她第三次访问该播客。在我们的第一次谈话中，我们深入探讨了创始人主导的销售；在第二个例子中，我们绘制了 100 万美元至 1000 万美元的剧本。这次我们做了一些我在其他播客中从未见过的事情：一步步走过整个企业销售周期。大多数人认为这是五个步骤。 Jen 表示已经接近 15 了。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么标准的五阶段 CRM 管道是预测工具，而不是销售流程，以及真正的 15 步循环是什么样的
2、首次会议同时落地高管层和N-1层的“夹击模式”
3. 如何围绕给他们“阿尔法”制定两到三句话的信息
4. 如何在演示之前运行一次介绍性通话以获取最大程度的情报
5. 两到三天的试点结构，如何共同定义成功，以及何时对较长的试点收费而不是免费
6. 在不失去动力的情况下完成定价、采购、红线谈判和最终签署

episodes.title: OpenAI’s Head of Design: This is the best time in history to be a designer | Ian Silber
episodes.description:
Ian Silber is the head of product design at OpenAI, where he has led the design of ChatGPT, Codex, and all of OpenAI’s product experience for the past three years. Before OpenAI, he was at Artifact, the AI-powered news app built by the founders of Instagram. Prior to that, he spent eight years at Instagram, where he worked on products including Reels. Ian is one of the most consequential designers working in AI today, and he takes us inside how OpenAI designs ChatGPT, Codex, and the future of how we will interact with AI.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Ian believes this is the best time in history to be a product designer
2. Why engineers 10x’d with AI but design teams haven’t
3. What OpenAI looks for when hiring designers
4. “Just do less”: Ian’s counterintuitive advice to his designers
5. The future of ChatGPT as a super app
6. Where humans still win: user understanding, invention, and point of view
episodes.descriptionCN:
Ian Silber 是 OpenAI 的产品设计主管，过去三年他领导了 ChatGPT、Codex 的设计以及 OpenAI 的所有产品体验。在加入 OpenAI 之前，他曾在 Artifact 工作，这是一款由 Instagram 创始人开发的人工智能新闻应用程序。在此之前，他在 Instagram 工作了八年，负责开发包括 Reels 在内的产品。 Ian 是当今人工智能领域最有影响力的设计师之一，他带我们了解 OpenAI 如何设计 ChatGPT、Codex，以及我们与人工智能交互的未来。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么 Ian 认为这是历史上成为产品设计师的最佳时代
2. 为什么工程师十倍地使用人工智能，但设计团队却没有
3. OpenAI 在招聘设计师时看重什么
4.“少做一点”：伊恩给设计师的违反直觉的建议
5. ChatGPT 作为超级应用程序的未来
6. 人类仍然获胜的地方：用户理解、发明和观点

episodes.title: The playbook for building high-talent-density teams | Adam Ward, Head of Talent at Cursor
episodes.guest: Adam Ward, Head of Talent at Cursor
episodes.description:
Adam Ward is the Head of Talent at Cursor, one of the fastest-growing developer tools in history. Before joining Cursor, he founded Growth by Design, an independent recruiting and talent strategy firm that helped build teams at the most ambitious AI and technology companies in the world. Adam has spent more than 20 years building elite, high-talent-density teams across the industry and is widely regarded as one of the most effective and creative recruiters in tech.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Inside today’s “tale of two cities” talent market
2. Why the traditional recruiting funnel—what Adam calls the “funnel of doom”—leads to mediocre hires
3. Adam’s three-step playbook: scoping, mapping, and relentless pursuit
4. The worst question to ask when sourcing great talent
5. The rise of the forward deployed engineer—and how to become one
6. The biggest mistake founders make when hiring their first recruiter
episodes.descriptionCN:
Adam Ward 是 Cursor 的人才主管，Cursor 是历史上发展最快的开发工具之一。在加入 Cursor 之前，他创立了 Growth by Design，这是一家独立的招聘和人才战略公司，帮助世界上最雄心勃勃的人工智能和技术公司建立团队。 Adam 花了 20 多年的时间在整个行业建立了精英、高人才密度的团队，被广泛认为是科技领域最有效和最具创造力的招聘人员之一。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 当今“两城故事”人才市场的内部
2. 为什么传统的招聘渠道（亚当称之为“末日漏斗”）会导致招聘效果平庸
3. Adam 的三步剧本：界定范围、绘制地图和不懈追求
4. 寻找优秀人才时要问的最糟糕的问题
5. 前沿部署工程师的崛起——以及如何成为一名前沿部署工程师
6. 创始人在雇用第一位招聘人员时犯的最大错误

episodes.description:

Closing on what a more specific and less outrage-driven version of this debate could actually produce.

episodes.title: Why Astra Is the Most Significant and Confounding Model in a Very Long Time
episodes.description:
GPT-6 Astra lands with a viral launch video and wildly mixed first impressions, topping computer use and 3D benchmarks while trailing Fable 5.1 on front-end design and general intelligence indexes. NLW argues the disconnect comes from judging an opportunity model by efficiency-model standards, since Astra expands what becomes possible rather than improving existing workflows. Also covered: the shift toward hands-free ambient computer use, the Blender and 3D modeling explosion, and why this one will take months to fully understand.

episodes.description:
swyx catchs up with Quinn Slack, CEO of Amp, discusses how the company has fundamentally changed software development by embracing AI agents and removing traditional processes like mandatory code reviews (7:03).

The Shift to Cloud-Based Development: Quinn argues that local development is effectively dead. AMP uses "orbs"—sandboxed environments running in the cloud—which allow for greater parallelism, security, and zero friction, enabling developers to work on multiple tasks at once without hardware limitations (1:49 - 2:07, 19:48).
The End of Mandatory Code Review: Because AMP uses a highly trusted, small, and accountable team, they have eliminated mandatory code reviews. They favor a "meantime before recovery" approach, which allows them to ship fixes in minutes rather than waiting for lengthy review processes (7:03 - 8:17).
Mini-Apps and Personalizable Software: Quinn explains that AI agents act as the "ultimate settings screen." Instead of building complex off-the-shelf software with rigid configurations, AMP focuses on building ad-hoc, forkable software ("jellyware") that can be customized via code and agents by the end user (10:10 - 13:30, 32:04).
Operational Efficiency: AMP uses agents not just for coding but for operational tasks, such as staging complex data migrations and monitoring production logs, which reduces the need for constant human oversight (14:45 - 17:00).
Company Philosophy: Quinn reflects on the advantages of staying a small, profitable "SWAT team" of 20 people. He argues that in the era of AI, the overhead of large teams (like hiring massive numbers of PMs or marketers) is becoming unnecessary, allowing for a focus on high-quality, high-agency work (29:45 - 31:36).

What would a GPT-style foundation model for the **physical world** look like?
Note: this is a followup to
Just days after emerging from stealth, Accelerated Understanding co-founders Anima Anandkumar and Benedikt Jenik,  join us to explain their bet: that the universality and scale we’ve seen in language models can also emerge across physics. They’re building a single model designed to learn across very different physical systems—fluid dynamics, semiconductors, energy, and more—and they say their experiments are already showing something important: models trained across multiple areas of physics can outperform equally sized models trained on individual domains alone.

episodes.title: ⏭️ Forward Deployed: Voice AI on what works in 2026
episodes.description:
Voice agents are one of the hottest use cases in enterprise right now, but also one of the hardest to actually take live. Getting latency low enough to feel human without dumbing down the responses, making reliable tool calls to a CRM without dropping the customer mid-call, building fallback models for when your main provider goes down. None of it is as simple as the demos make it look.
Basil Chatha hosted a fireside chat with five eng leaders who deal with this stuff every day: Basia Sudol (Head of Enterprise Solutions, Decagon), Varun Singh (CPTO, Daily), Steven Diaz (FDE Manager, Vapi), Tyler D'Silva (Founding FDE, Retell AI), and Sudarshan Kamath (Founder, Smallest AI).
We get into why nobody serious is shipping real-time voice-to-voice yet, why LLMs forget the middle of your prompt (and what that does to your architecture), why a giant prompt quietly destroys your unit economics, and why voice agent costs are now being compared directly against human labor.
Plus the stuff nobody warns you about: turn-taking, HIPAA constraints, why outbound is easier than inbound, why getting an exec to actually like the voice can be harder than any model problem, and more!

episodes.title: Simulating Humanity: from Generative Agents to 8 Billion Digital Twins — Joon Sung Park, Simile AI
episodes.description:
Next episode → Language Agents: From Reasoning to Acting, with Shunyu Yao and Harrison Chase:
From creating Smallville, the landmark Generative Agents experiment that showed AI characters could remember, plan, socialize, and develop emergent behaviors, to now building foundation models of human behavior, Joon Sung Park is trying to answer a much bigger question: what if we could simulate the world before making decisions in it? In this episode, the Simile co-founder and CEO joins us to unpack the path from generative agents to digital twins, why today’s frontier models still fail to capture how humans actually behave, and what it would take to eventually simulate all 8 billion people on Earth.
We go deep on Simile’s approach to modeling human behavior: long-form interviews, observational and transaction data, randomized controlled trials, population-level and individual-level models, and post-training on the causal mechanisms behind why people make decisions. Joon explains how his research created digital twins that reproduced human behavior and attitudes 85% as accurately as people reproduced their own responses, why models optimized to be rational can be bad simulations of irrational humans, and why understanding “social physics” may require changing model weights rather than simply prompting frontier LLMs.
We also explore the much larger ambition behind simulation: testing products and policies before deploying them, finding counterintuitive paths toward desired outcomes, modeling emergent behavior across entire societies, and potentially tackling problems like climate change, democratic instability, and UBI. Joon reflects on scaling laws for simulation, the economics of data-center-scale simulated worlds, the connection to Thomas Schelling and psychohistory, why simulation is surprisingly similar to painting, and whether we might already be living in one.
We discuss:
• How Smallville and the Generative Agents paper led to Simile

episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.

我们曾经相信，有 10X 工程师的存在，但也曾经存在一些争议。现在显然有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有完全适应这一点。
@naval：我曾经因为说有 10X 工程师而在 Twitter 上受到攻击，因为它违背了人人平等的平等理念。但现实是，当你在创意领域运作时——当你在知识领域和虚拟数字领域运作时——它甚至还不到 10 倍。它是 100 倍或 1,000 倍，而且一直都是。
Satoshi，Notch��JavaScript 的发明者，世界上的 Brendan Eichs。约翰·卡马克.这些是 1000 倍的程序员。
更不用说你选择正确的工作还是错误的工作，这是一个无穷大的差异。而且不一定是更好的程序员，只是一个对首先要做什么有更好判断的人。
现在，由于人工智能的影响力，它的争议显然减少了。

episodes.description:
I run this episode solo. I explain local AI in plain terms: the model runs on hardware I control, and a cloud model runs somewhere else. I map the four pieces of the local AI landscape — the model, the warehouse, the software, and the workflow — and I define the words that beginners meet first: parameters, tokens, context window, quantization, and GGUF. I walk through the Google open model stack (Gemma 4, Google AI Edge, LiteRT-LM, AI Edge Gallery), compare the other open model families, and show three ways to run a model today. I close with a first workflow you can copy and three startup ideas that use local AI as the wedge.
And a special thank you to Google for supporting the podcast.
Get the full guide to running local AI:

Key Points
• Ask whether the model is good enough for the job, and the business opportunities become clear.
• Local AI has four pieces: the model, the warehouse (Hugging Face), the software (LM Studio or Ollama), and the workflow you build around them.
• Gemma 4 E4B is my practical starting point; E2B fits phones and older machines.
• Hybrid architecture wins: local does the private first pass, cloud does the heavy reasoning, and a human approves anything important.
• Start with one repeated workflow — one folder, one model, one output — and run it 10 times.
• I see a 24-month window to build local-AI-native software for verticals that still run early-2000s tools.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. The Four Pieces of the Local AI Landscape I break the space into the model (the brain file, such as Gemma, Llama, or Mistral), the warehouse (Hugging Face), the software that runs the model (LM Studio or Ollama), and the workflow (the product around all of it). Underneath the tools sit Llama.cpp and MLX, and for shipping on-device apps in the Google ecosystem you reach Google AI Edge and LiteRT-LM. On Hugging Face I read a model card slowly and look for six things: purpose, size, license, hardware, supported inputs, and quantized files.
2. The Vocabulary That Matters I define parameters as the internal weights, where more parameters give more capacity and cost more memory: 2B and 4B for edge devices and fast workflows, 12B as a middle ground, and 26B or 31B for workstation territory. I define tokens, the context window, quantization (Q4 for easier running, Q8 for more quality), and GGUF as the common local file format. I suggest you start on a phone or a spare 2021 laptop and keep your money for later.
3. The Google Open Model Stack Gemma is Google's open model family, and Gemma 4 targets efficient local and on-device use across E2B, E4B, 12B, and 26B/31B. The specialized models deserve attention: EmbeddingGemma for search by meaning, FunctionGemma for tool use and structured function calling, PaliGemma for vision, ShieldGemma for safety, and Gemma Scope for interpretability. Around the models sit Google AI Edge, LiteRT-LM, AI Edge Gallery, and Gemini plus Google Cloud for frontier-level reasoning.
4. Three Ways to Run Gemma Today Path one is LM Studio: download the app, search for Gemma 4, pick E4B or E2B, grab the quantized GGUF, and paste real customer notes into a chat to feel the value. Then start the LM Studio local server so your scripts and prototypes call the model through localhost. Path two is Ollama with a local API on port 11434, and path three is Google AI Edge with LiteRT-LM for Android, iOS, web, desktop, and edge apps. I also give a RAM cheat sheet: 8 GB stays small, 16 GB runs useful experiments, 32 GB opens larger workflows, and a strong GPU makes the bigger models realistic.

3. 从 SEO 到 AEO 再到代理执行 我将这一转变分为三个步骤。 SEO 询问 Google 是否理解该页面。 AEO 询问 AI 是否引用答案。 WebMCP 询问代理是否完成了工作，这就是数十亿美元将易手的地方。
4. 登录状态作为身份验证层工具以浏览器会话为条件。 Vince 登录并显示完整的工具列表，他注销后仍保留三个工具。代理共享会话，因此登录涵盖了访问权限，并且 API 密钥和令牌不参与流程。
5. 代理原生地图 Vince 详细介绍了他的图表：原始 API 和经典 MCP 服务器保持无头状态，计算机使用和浏览器 MCP 读取屏幕截图和整个 DOM，应用内代理将用户保留在您的产品中。 WebMCP 位于中间。它为应用程序代理提供了功能，而用户则带来了已经保存其上下文和内存的代理。
6. WebMCP 最适合的地方 Vince 将兼容性驱动的商业以及相机系统等复杂的商店称为首要用例。接下来是 SaaS 管理、分析和营销控制���。保险和银行自助服务等受监管部门可以提供指导用户的只读工具，而内部工具则为创始人提供了一个安全的起点。
7. 创业想法 1：WebMCP 转换代理机构 我推荐一家代理机构，让无聊的商业网站做好代理准备：律师事务所、暖通空调和家庭服务、医疗水疗中心和牙医。您提供 V1 工具，例如请求报价和预约咨询，收取 2,000 到 10,000 美元的设置费用，并每月保留几百到 700 美元的费用用于监控和评估。 Vince 建议您将其作为跨 MCP、WebMCP 和内部工具的软件包进行销售，以便在标准成熟时您拥有专家席位。
8. 创业想法 2：代理神秘顾客 第二个想法测试代理是否完成了重要的旅程：购买连帽衫、预约咨询、提出索赔、重新订购商品。客户会收到一份定期报告，了解代理在哪里停滞、哪些描述读起来很差、缺少哪些工具以及转换风险在哪里。定价接近每月 100 美元到几百美元，将重复修复转化为软件，并将其与转换机构配对作为主要来源。

episodes.description:
I sit down with Billy Howell for an inside look at a real business that runs on Grok Bot agent teams. Billy tests hundreds of tools for The Rundown, and he uses Grok Bot to run his local newsletter, The Arlington Bagel, which goes to 6,000 readers every Thursday. He walks me through his chief of staff bot, his research and sales agents, and the routines that move work forward while he sleeps. We cover the token math, the four-week plan he follows, and the business models that fit this tool best: newsletters, directories, and Shopify stores. You leave with a setup you can copy for one project this month.

42:50 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• Keep one project per Grok Bot account, so context stays clean and tokens stay available.
• Start with a chief of staff bot, and let it audit your business and name the first three agents.
• Follow the four weeks: build the team, execute, hire and fire, then automate.
• Ask each agent for a five-line brief: what shipped, what is stuck, what needs you.
• Move repeatable steps into scripts or make com, and keep agent tokens for high value work.
• Newsletters and directories give the easiest entry, and the two models feed each other.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. One Project, One Agent Team
Billy runs each Grokbot account on a single mission. Several businesses in one account cause context bloat, slow work, and heavy token use. He pays $200 a month for a second account that holds his Shopify experiment alone.
2. Design as a Feature
Grokbot gives you a limited set of agents, and Billy counts roughly 76 to 88 shape and color combinations. One thread per bot works like a direct message to a teammate, so he finds each agent fast and saves switching costs.
3. The Chief of Staff Audit
Billy picks a chief of staff first and connects it to Notion, Slack, and Gmail. On day one it takes stock of the business and names the top three agents that drive revenue. His audit produces a research agent, a sales agent, and a Beehive platform expert.
4. Build, Execute, Expand, Automate
Week one builds the team. Week two stays on execution alone. Week three fills the real gaps, such as an inbox agent. Week four adds routines, so the team moves the ball while Billy sleeps.
5. Routines and Five-Line Briefs
Each agent sends a short daily or weekly report to the chief of staff: what shipped, what is stuck, and what needs the human. Five lines keep tokens and context tight, and the chief of staff routes the rest of the work.
6. Teach Agents to Review Like You
Billy runs adversarial QA loops with a panel of subagents across three rounds, and output moves from about 50 percent done to about 90 percent done. He then turns a feedback thread into a skill, so another agent reviews work in his own style.
7. The Newsletter Machine
A research bot checks his source list twice a week and fills Notion cards with restaurant news and events. A make.com step formats each blurb the same way every week, and Beehive sends the issue on Thursday. His sales agent watches the Gmail inbox, prices the ad slots, builds a sales sheet, and found a local bagel shop sponsor this week.
8. Directories, Shopify, and the Site Builder Stack
Billy runs a stack of Cloudflare, Porkbun, Astro, and GitHub, and he shipped a live booking page from the beach in two or three hours. For directories, a research agent writes a brand page as markdown each day and a coding agent publishes it. He calls a newsletter plus a directory the lowest barrier entry point for a Grokbot business.

1.一个项目，一个代理团队
Billy 在一项任务中管理每个 Grokbot 帐户。一个账户中的多项业务会导致上下文膨胀、工作缓慢和大量令牌使用。他每月支付 200 美元购买第二个帐户，该帐户仅用于他的 Shopify 实验。
2. 设计作为一项功能
Grokbot 为您提供了一组有限的代理，Billy 统计了大约 76 到 88 种形状和颜色组合。每个机器人一个线程的工作方式就像向队友发送直接消息，因此他可以快速找到每个代理并节省转换成本。
3. 参谋长审计
Billy 首先选择一位幕僚长，并将其连接到 Notion、Slack 和 Gmail。第一天，它会对业务进行盘点，并列出最能带来收入的三大代理商。他的审计产生了一名研究代理、一名销售代理和一名 Beehive 平台专家。
4. 构建、执行、扩展、自动化
第一周建立团队。第二周只专注于执行。第三周填补了真正的空白，例如收件箱代理。第四周增加了例行公事，因此球队在比利睡觉时移动球。
5. 例程和五行摘要
每个代理每天或每周都会向参谋长发送一份简短的报告：什么已发货、什么被卡住以及什么需要人工。五行保持令牌和上下文的紧密性，参谋长负责安排其余的工作。
6. 教代理人像你一样审查
Billy 与一组子代理一起在三轮中运行对抗性 QA 循环，输出从完成的 50% 左右提高到完成的 90% 左右。然后，他将反馈线索转化为一项技能，以便另一位代理以他自己的风格审查工作。
7. 新闻通讯机
研究机器人每周两次检查他的来源列表，并在概念卡中填写餐厅新闻和活动。 make.com 步骤每周都会以相同的方式格式化每个简介，Beehive 会在周四发送该问题。他的销售代理会监视 Gmail 收件箱、为广告位定价、制作销售表，并于本周找到了一家当地百吉饼店的赞助商。
8. 目录、Shopify 和 Site Builder Stack
